items.title: Mike Vax interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 29, 2022
items.q: The interviewee discusses Stan Getz's leadership style in response to a question comparing him to 'Count' Basie, but does not mention any personal interaction with Count Basie.

ctx.x: I think it’s a bit of both. I don’t think — the responsibility of the lead trumpet player is that you have to make sure things are going because in a professional situation if things aren’t happening in the band there are times when the leader is going to blame the lead trumpet player. You know? And yeah there are times, especially with John Von Ohlen and John Worster that we talked about different charts and it wasn’t like John was saying well Vax you’re not coming in right, or I was saying well you’re not…

A number of Basie alums have talked about how the Count was sort of a hands off — he didn’t say anything unless something was really bad. And I wondered if Stan was like that or was he more hands-on and how did he deal with any, I guess I’ll call them discipline issues?

Well first of all Stan was very hands-on. And to play in that band you had to be 110% all the time. You know, the concentration level — I’ll tell you — this is a great one. I don’t remember when this happened but it was something where, you know any of the band leaders, they’re basically going to play tunes from the last album and tunes that made them famous. And so they get into this thing of different tours you’re going to play almost the same charts every night. You know. And sometimes the band is getting oooo…

items.title: Mike Vax interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 29, 2022
items.q: And so he really believed, and he was the first band leader to bring his band into schools on a regular basis, and from that Maynard did it and Woody did it and even Basie a little bit.

ctx.x: I want to read a brief quote from our interview. And there’s not a question here but I just wanted to share this with you. He said, “When you’re twelve years old and you can hit a double high C your ego inflates pretty fast. I heard Maynard Ferguson playing high notes on the end of a tune so I just played a high note on the end of everything. It didn’t matter what the chord was, I just played a double high C because my friends were all going ‘all right’ and they’d high five me.”

I mean that’s so true. And it’s an interesting phenomenon I guess. There are some people, like Wayne was really a natural from the beginning. I was sort of a natural but I wasn’t one of those guys that just had it when I was young. And I had to work really hard to get where some other trumpet players already were, you know in high school and stuff and junior high even. And so I just — I had decided probably by the time I was 14 or 15 I want to be a trumpet player. You know? Just I want to be a trumpet player. And…

still alive, Norm Tompach, who really got me into the jazz thing. He had written for Basie and Woody and he was the leader of the Fort Ord Army Band at one point. And so he was important and then in college Gordon Finlay, who’d been the solo cornetist with the Navy band in Washington for 20 years. I studied with him. And these people made me work. You know I practiced a lot and I practiced what they wanted me to. I didn’t just sit and play tunes or whatever, although I did that afterwards. In fact even when I was…
